K1.1.title: 1. owned -- the holder carries the disposal obligation: dispose exactly once, on every path.

K1.2.title: 2. borrowed -- no obligation; validity is bounded by the borrow's source set (K2).

K1.3.title: 3. moved-from -- the obligation has transferred out; the binding is unreadable until reassigned, and discharge machinery skips it (§28.8.1).

K1.4.title: 4. maybe-consumed -- the K7 join of owned with moved-from or explicitly-disposed; unreadable until reassigned (a reassignment displaces per path and leaves the binding owned, §28.3 State match); scope-end disposal is per-path.

K1.5.title: 5. Atoms. Fresh productions are owned: new, reference-typed collection literals, owned-returning calls, move results, owned operator results. Reads of storage lend: a field, property, indexer, or slot read is a borrow whose source is the storage's holder. Reads of named bindings lend unless the position consumes (K3): an unmarked read of an owned binding is a borrow of the binding. Calls lend by default: an instance method's plain (non-owned) class-typed return is a borrow whose source is the receiver -- sound jointly with the callee-side admission rules (K2.4). A static callee's plain class- or interface-typed return is admissible only where the declared type announces the classification (type-announced, K2.4/K6.2), and is otherwise rejected at the declaration (the static-return rule, Factory methods below). (The Producers table below is the worked enumeration; the announcement table beside it is the per-callee-kind matrix for calls.)

K1.6.title: 6. The runtime-managed exemption; the trivial-dispose ceremony exemption. Values of runtime-managed type (string, Type, boxed value types, function values) and of ordinary value type carry no classification and no obligation; owned markers over them are inadmissible or erased per instantiation (§28.1). Trivial-dispose class instances (§28.9) carry the classification and the free obligation, but the obligation's user-visible content is empty and its discharge is never demanded of the program: any undischarged trivial-dispose value is freed silently by the compiler at its owner's release point -- no warning (the ceremony exemption), no user code (the class has none to run; the free sets the disposed flag, §28.2). The exemption is ceremony-only: the borrow half of the machinery -- source sets, escape checks, the freeze -- is demanded over trivial-sourced references everywhere, and every rule of this chapter reads them by its letter.

K1.7.title: 7. One holder. An obligation has exactly one holder at a time; every transfer moves it, never copies it. Copy-semantics holders (record fields) therefore cannot hold obligations (§28.5).

K2.1.title: 1. Weakest source bounds. A borrow is valid only where every source in its set is live; equivalently, it is bounded by its weakest source.

K2.2.title: 2. Union under composition. Joins, ?? and arm meets, transitive re-borrows, and frame carriage combine borrows by taking the union of their source sets.

K2.3.title: 3. Escape must be bounded. A borrow may not reach a holder -- a binding of wider scope, a field, a collection, a frame, a return -- whose lifetime the checker cannot bound by the borrow's source set. Where scopes are statically comparable (locals, temporaries, loop back edges), violation is rejected. Where they are not, an admission is made only under K4's posture: a structural, decidable check at the site plus a recorded residual obligation with a named backstop (§28.3, §28.11).

K2.4.title: 4. Signature-level re-establishment. A callee's declared signature announces its result's source set -- the type-announced classification: read off the declared, pre-substitution type, K6.2 being the frame instance -- as a function of the call's receiver and arguments -- the bare-type-parameter source set, the deferred-activation frame's carried sources -- and every caller re-establishes the set against its own actuals. A borrow whose source no caller could re-establish (a scope-bound local, a temporary, a parameter source the signature does not announce) may not be returned.

K3.13.title: 13. Marker economy. A consume is spelled by the transfer marker (move x) except at a marker-free position, where the target or keyword already announces it -- the table's Spelling column is the definition site of which is which. An unmarked read of a class-typed binding never consumes: var b := a; is always a borrow for class-typed a. (Move-only value types move on unmarked assignment and plain parameter passing, per §15.3's own scope note; K3.12.) Fresh producers need no marker anywhere (no live binding is invalidated).

K3.14.title: 14. Affinity. An owned value that reaches its scope's end undischarged and not moved-from is disposed there implicitly; the implicit drop of a plain-var local or undischarged owned parameter carries the must-use warning (a lint over a sound program; not at a trivial-dispose value -- K1.6's ceremony exemption).

K3.15.title: 15. Edge parity. The exception edge performs the same implicit disposal as the normal edge, on the single establishment-ordered cleanup stack; the only difference is the lint. Unbound temporaries join the same stack at their production.

K4.title: Kills, site-announcement, and the backstop posture

K4.1.title: 1. The backstop. Disposal is idempotent and flag-setting; in checked disposal mode (§28.2) any later use through any alias faults deterministically as DisposedAccessException, and unchecked mode is the same language with the check elided. This is the runtime backstop every trust admission names.

K4.2.title: 2. Site-announced kills. A kill that is both keyword-visible at the kill site and flag-backstopped is site-announced, and is permitted while borrows of the value live: the announcement is the reader's notice and the flag is the safety net. The closed set is exactly the consume table's three rows tagged K4.2 -- explicit disposal (Dispose(), a direct DisposeAsync() call, or the discard), throw x, and Pattern B await of an owned operand (a borrowed operand's award spends the task and kills nothing, §30.5) -- with each kill's post-state and disposal moment in the table's columns.

K4.3.title: 3. Recorded trust, or nothing. Where an admission's temporal guarantee can neither be statically compared (K2.3) nor flag-backstopped -- the domain clause (§28.3's field-store bullet, clause 4): a borrowed-from object transferred to, or made reachable from, another domain stays alive, so no flag is ever set -- the rule must either reject statically or carry an individually recorded trust clause. The recorded clauses (field-held, collection-held, comparer-held and frame-held borrows versus domain transfer; §28.3, stdlib §4, §30.1) are the model's honest limit, and no new admission may be made without recording its clause or its backstop. No clause covers a static-held borrow, and none is needed: a borrow of anything but static storage is stored into no static field or static property (§28.3's Static stores) -- across domains the flag is no backstop, so the always-live holder admits only what lives as long as it does. (A borrow held inside an object a static references is that object's field-, collection- or frame-held clause, with §22.12 rule 4's confinement obligation where the static is warned.) The recorded set is enumerable, and the trust-admission report mode (§28.3) enumerates it at every site.

K5.1.title: 1. the family-1 transfers and owning-iterator yield return (the table's rows K3.1-K3.4, K3.7, K3.12) are frozen -- each fails (ii): an obligation-moving kill sets no flag, and its surviving borrows' referents are neither flagged nor guaranteed intact for the borrows' whole life;

K5.2.title: 2. drop-on-overwrite of a binding (row K3.11) is frozen although it disposes -- it fails (i): the reassignment is not keyword-visible as a kill of the old value, and the flag it does set is irrelevant once (i) fails;

K5.3.title: 3. the K4.2 site-announced kills (rows K3.5, K3.8, K3.9) are unfrozen -- each satisfies (i), and satisfies (ii) wherever the surviving borrows are backstopped by the kill's own flag, which is every case but the two recorded in clauses 7 and 8;

K5.4.title: 4. a Pattern A chaining return await x (row K3.6) is unfrozen by the criterion: (i) holds -- the return await keywords are the kill site (§30.5) -- and (ii) holds because every borrow that survives the kill has its referent left intact and disposal-tracked: the new holder (the outer task) cannot dispose the chained task before the body, finally blocks included, completes, so no surviving borrow needs a flag;

K5.5.title: 5. the freeze is body-local by construction -- the clause bounds what liveness means, not what is frozen: liveness is the backward dataflow over one body, borrows are traced through using var pins, an argument or operand of the same full expression evaluated before the consume and used by its call or operator (§28.3), live closures, locals of borrow-bearing record or inline-array type or of choice types that hold borrows (§9.7; §15.1.2; §35.4's holds-borrows property), and locals -- a for desugaring's hidden __source (§29.2) included -- holding an iterator or enumerator frame or a lazy query (K6), each a live local borrow of every source the frame carries, transitively through the frames and closures it carries, as a live closure value is of its captures' sources, the frame's own disposal -- explicit, at a using var's scope end, or K3.14's auto-drop -- counting as a use, since a partially-consumed frame's disposal runs its pending cleanup (§29.7) (§28.3 Frame locals); and this is why a closure may not consume its captured owned bindings (K2 + decidability);

K5.6.title: 6. fields and collection slots are not frozen -- the clause bounds what the freeze's subject is: slot aliases are not body-local, and a slot kill disposes -- the K4 backstop is real there; the slot kill by move is instead governed by K4.3's domain clause (§28.3, §28.7, §28.11);

K5.7.title: 7. a §28.14 storage admission freezes the admitted captures against the site-announced kills as well -- a derivation from (ii), not an exception: the surviving borrow lives in a stored callback whose invocation site is statically invisible at the kill, and the storage admission's promise is a fully static bound, so a runtime flag is not an admissible backstop for it -- stated with its reason at §28.14, under axiom A11's forms (the freeze's subject is the captured binding: a captured or passed borrow of a slot's current value -- class- or interface-typed, or a span over it -- keeps clause 6's runtime-checked posture under this admission as under any other, §28.14 scoped construction);

K5.8.title: 8. a §30.12 guard's site-announced kills are frozen while borrows sourced from the guard live -- likewise a derivation from (ii): killing a guard sets the disposed flag on the guard, while the surviving borrows reference the lock's interior, on which no flag is set, the lock released out from under them -- stated with its reason at §30.12.

K6.1.title: 1. The bound. Carried sources must outlive the frame's bound: settlement for a task (§30.1); completion or disposal for an iterator frame (§29.4, §29.7); the single consumption point for a lazy query, which is thereby affine (§29.11); an iterator frame minted over an owned or move-only parameter keeps the iterator frame's bound and is affine by the same rule (§29.8).

K6.2.title: 2. Announcement by declared type. Frame-carrying classification is type-announced -- keyed on the callee's declared, pre-substitution return type: a Task-family type, a §29.3/§30.7 iterable or enumerator interface, a lazy query -- and every caller re-establishes the carried set against its own actuals (K2.4). This is what admits returning a composed frame, and what rejects a returned frame carrying a scope-bound local, using var, or temporary.

K6.3.title: 3. Containers: calls mint, storage lends. A call whose declared return type is mint-announcing -- a Task-family type, or an iterable-family type (a §29.3/§30.7 iterable or enumerator interface, or a lazy query) -- produces a fresh owned frame at every call site; a read of frame storage (property, field, slot) lends a borrow of the storage; callee-side, the unmarked mint-announcing return type transfers the container like an owned return (axiom A15's self-returning enumerator excepted).

K6.4.title: 4. Frames versus the freeze. Frame-held borrows live in the frame, not in any local borrow binding. A task's are not traced by K5: their outlives-obligation is the K4.3-recorded settlement clause (§30.1), discharged trivially by awaiting before any source's scope exits and structurally by TaskScope; the abandonment idioms carry the residual explicitly, under §30.1's bans on a holds-borrows parameter and on a caller-sourced holds-borrows local across a suspension, a binding an async lambda captures from its enclosing scope among them. An iterator, enumerator or lazy-query frame is traced by K5.5 through the local that holds it, as a closure value is through its local: its carried sources are frozen while that local is live against the silent kills, the site-announced kills staying unfrozen under their flag, which reaches a read through a span the frame may hold (§29.4) as it reaches any member access (§28.2); the K4.3 frame clause still names the residual for a frame no traced local holds.

K6.5.title: 5. Interaction with K8. A frame sourced by an unbound temporary must itself be consumed to its bound within the same full expression; a frame that escapes the expression is rejected -- the reject-not-extend posture.

K7.1.title: 1. owned ⊓ owned = owned, obligation carried forward (for expression arms: exactly one arm's value exists at runtime, so exactly one obligation);

K7.2.title: 2. borrowed ⊓ borrowed = borrowed, carrying the union of the arms' source sets (K2.2);

K7.3.title: 3. owned ⊓ borrowed = rejected -- no single state is correct, and demoting owned would silently drop an obligation; the program equalizes the arms first;

K7.4.title: 4. owned ⊓ moved-from and owned ⊓ explicitly-disposed = maybe-consumed -- unreadable after the join, no flow around a back edge into a use; scope-end disposal per-path;

K7.5.title: 5. null-literal and bottom-typed (throw) arms absorb to the other arm's state.

K8.1.title: 1. Unbound owned temporaries are disposed at their full expression's end, after their uses, in reverse production order -- on the normal edge as on the exception edge, where the pass runs during unwinding.

K8.2.title: 2. Conditions and guards are per-evaluation boundaries: temporaries never accumulate across iterations.

K8.3.title: 3. A case scrutinee's boundary is the whole construct -- pattern bindings are borrows of the scrutinee, and the temporary survives arm selection, guard evaluation, and the selected arm's completion -- in statement position exactly as in expression position.

K8.4.title: 4. A temporary is an admissible borrow source only within its boundary; a borrow or frame that would escape it is rejected, never lifetime-extended -- the language has no general lifetime-extension mechanism (§9.7; rationale §5.24). The escapes rejected are every escape K2.3 can compare -- among them a binding, store, capture, return or yield return of the borrow in the producing body -- and every retention a declaration announces -- among them a returned frame (K6.5), a frame carrying the borrow taken by an owned parameter or owning slot (Task.FireAndForget, §28.3), a borrow-bearing record's field or a holds-borrows choice's payload (§9.7, §35.4), a scoped parameter (§28.14), and a ref or out location. A plain parameter announces none: a callee that stores it holds the borrow under the borrowed-field rule's or the borrowing-collection store rule's recorded residual (§28.3, §28.11), and the temporary is still disposed at its boundary (K8.1).

K8.5.title: 5. A binding atom (§17.15) is the boundary for its own bindings: a binding whose initializer is an owned production is a named unbound owned temporary whose boundary is the atom -- disposed at the atom's completion if undischarged, after the body's evaluation, in reverse clause order; clause 4 applies to the atom boundary verbatim.

K9.title: Fields are object state, not scope state

K9.1.title: 1. every plain read of an owned field lends (K1.5); the only owned read of an owned field or an owning slot is the replacing move (§28.8.1): move x.f with e -- and move coll[i] with e -- stores the owned value e into the location and yields the displaced value, owned, in one step with no intermediate state; where the location's declared type is nullable, move x.f alone stores null;

K9.2.title: 2. an owned location never holds a hole: a non-nullable owned field or owning slot holds a live value at every instant, a nullable one holds a live value or null, and the moved-from state is a state of bindings only (K1) -- so no path carries a restoration obligation, no code can observe a location between a take and a store, and a destructor cascade meets live values and nulls only;

K9.3.title: 3. a constructor's move is governed by definite assignment before first assignment (§7.9); a destructor body reads and takes the fields of the object it tears down as any other body does -- the replacing move, or the bare take at a nullable field -- and may dispose one its own class declares early (§28.6), the cascade's later call being the no-op; no body takes a non-nullable owned location bare (§28.8.1);

K9.4.title: 4. static owned storage -- a static owned field, and the slots of a static readonly owning inline array (§22.12 note (h)) -- admits no move, no slot store and no explicit disposal: it is the always-live source (K2), whose referent every borrow of it may be held against as process-lived, so it is neither taken nor replaced and is disposed only by the exit pass (§28.8.1, §22.12, §22.13, §28.6);

K9.5.title: 5. drop-on-overwrite (K3.11) is RHS-first, so a throwing RHS leaves the slot untouched and still-owned, and a throwing disposer of the displaced value leaves that value at the slot, logically disposed, to the slot's next release point (§28.7); the replacing move evaluates its replacement first by the same order, and its exchange disposes nothing -- the displaced value is its result.
